method: My method was to follow the two threads — Ryan's backward history and Cubitt's deep history — while returning constantly to the one question, projection versus illumination, and keeping the quotes that answered it. Then I read them against my own project, which is, by coincidence, literally about projection and a body.
related_work:
Ryan opened with a definition I have been carrying since: projection is light plus an obstacle plus a wall, and the oldest projection is a fire casting shadows inside a cave — which is already Plato's cave before Plato. The etymology makes the same point: pro-ject means to throw forward, sub-ject to be thrown under, ob-ject to be thrown before you, re-ject to be thrown back. Then came the question that organised the whole session. Looking at the giant 3D cat billboard in Shinjuku, or Tokyo's multi-screen walls, Ryan asked whether we were seeing projection at all — or illumination, a screen glowing on its own. This is the test I keep applying now to everything I look at.

The history he ran through was told backwards, from Kentridge's projected drawings at the Goodman Gallery — one drawing sold for £475,000, and the large image is assembled from single drawings, a logic that kept recurring — back through Josef Svoboda's 1957 Brussels pavilion, where several analogue projectors were synchronised into a rear-projected grid around live performers, the Eames's Glimpses of the USA in a Fuller dome, IBM's Think pavilion at the 1964 New York fair, Stan VanDerBeek's Movie-Drome where you lie under a dome of 8mm and 16mm projectors, Le Corbusier and Varèse's Poème électronique, Piscator and the Bauhaus stage in the 1920s, and finally the nineteenth-century panorama, a huge rotating painting that simulated travel and, Ryan said, anticipated early cinema. Two of his asides stayed with me. One: 'every art experience is an immersive experience — if you go and look at a painting, that's interactive,' a reminder not to confuse immersive with virtual reality. The other: everyone borrows from everyone, which is fine as long as the academic honesty is kept.

Sean Cubitt's half reached further back and made the argument sharper. Speer's 1933 searchlights over the Zeppelin field, he said, were both a projection and an immersive experience — projection and immersion are not opposites but two dimensions of the same thing. Immersion, he argued, starts with the night sky and with the Lascaux caves forty thousand years ago, where you were 'led by a flickering torch' past animals on the wall, 'not unlike the flicker of cinema.' He kept the scale human: a Japanese folding screen is immersive in your own living room, and for the Yolngu 'watching a fire is itself an immersive experience' — small, indoor, surrounded by people — where Refik Anadol's projections are instead built to overwhelm you. Then the cave returned. Cinema, quoting Flann O'Brien, is 'a dark sort of place where people go to stare at the wall,' and Cubitt pushed it to its end: 'any kind of immersion is fictional. It is a simulation. It is a lie. It is pure appearance and reality is elsewhere.' Projection has a second, colder meaning too — it turns things into objects, the way naming a star or focusing a lens (the French word for lens is objectif) turns something vast into one thing to be looked at. That is where the male gaze becomes a human gaze, and where the subject and the object end up bound together.
conclusion_future_work: The homework is a choice: write a short reflective piece on the history or current role of projection, or make a piece intended for projection or digital screening. I am leaning towards making, because the projection-versus-illumination question feels like something to test with my hands rather than describe. Next week is speculative design and planetary art, with Benjamin Bratton's The Terraforming and Robert Gerard Pietrusko's A Satellite Symphony to read beforehand. Whatever I make, I want to carry one question from this session into it: is this projection, or is it just a screen glowing in the dark
results_discussion:
The distinction between projection and illumination is the thing I will not be able to unsee. I had been treating a screen as a screen, but they are not the same: one throws light onto something, the other glows on its own, and the difference matters for what a piece claims to be. Ryan's refusal to equate immersive with virtual reality was quietly deflating in the best way — it took a fashionable word and gave it back its plain meaning, so that looking hard at a painting counts. Cubitt then resolved the apparent tension: projection and immersion are two dimensions of the same thing, which is why the cave is the whole story in miniature — a flame, a wall, and people staring at shadows, unable to see the fire.

That last image unsettles me in a way I like, because it is also a description of cinema, and maybe of my own work. 'Any kind of immersion is a lie, pure appearance, and reality is elsewhere' is a warning, but for a maker it is also a permission: if immersion is constructed, then I get to choose what to construct. This landed directly on the dance-and-projection piece I have been circling with my friend. A dancer's body is the object being thrown before an audience, and the projected image is the projection thrown onto it — the etymology made the piece feel like an argument about subject and object that I had not noticed I was making. And Cubitt's human-scale examples — the folding screen, the fire — cut against the reflex that bigger and more overwhelming is more immersive, which is exactly the question I now want my own piece to answer.
title: Projection, illumination, and the cave
introduction: This week's lecture was about projection and immersive environments, and it kept circling one question: when you look at a screen, are you seeing projection — light thrown onto a surface — or illumination, a screen that simply glows? Ryan Bishop walked the history of projection backwards, from William Kentridge to the nineteenth-century panorama, and the guest speaker Sean Cubitt took it much further back, to the oldest projector there is: firelight throwing shadows on a cave wall.
